question: Under MCA 37-51-325, an individually licensed Montana broker who is not covered under a firm's group policy must carry errors and omissions insurance with what minimum per-claim and annual aggregate limits?
choice_a: $50,000 per claim / $100,000 aggregate
choice_b: $100,000 per claim / $300,000 aggregate
choice_c: $250,000 per claim / $500,000 aggregate
choice_d: $1,000,000 per claim / $1,000,000 aggregate
explanation: MCA 37-51-325 sets a $100,000 per-claim / $300,000 annual aggregate minimum for an individual E&O policy (the same floor applies to the board-approved group policy). $50,000/$100,000 is too low to satisfy the statute, and the $250,000/$500,000 and $1,000,000/$1,000,000 figures overstate the individual-policy minimum (the higher aggregate is the firm-policy floor, not the individual one).

question: Under MCA 37-51-325, what is the maximum per-claim deductible allowed on an individual or group errors and omissions policy without special board approval, compared to a firm policy?
choice_a: There is no deductible cap for any type of E&O policy in Montana
choice_b: $10,000 for an individual or group policy; $2,500 for a firm policy
choice_c: $2,500 for an individual or group policy; up to $10,000 (or more with board approval of the firm's financial capacity) for a firm policy
choice_d: $1,000 for all policy types, with no exceptions
explanation: MCA 37-51-325 caps the deductible at $2,500 per claim for individual and group policies, while a firm policy may carry a deductible up to $10,000 (or higher if the board approves based on the firm's demonstrated financial capacity). The reversed figures in choice C, and the claims of no cap or a flat $1,000 cap, misstate the statute.

question: A Montana broker's E&O policy expires. Under MCA 37-51-325, what extended reporting period must the policy automatically provide after termination or cancellation, and what additional optional period may the licensee request?
choice_a: An automatic 365-day period only, with no optional extension available
choice_b: No automatic extended reporting period; the licensee must purchase all tail coverage separately
choice_c: An automatic 30-day period, plus an optional 90-day extension
choice_d: An automatic 60-day extended reporting period, plus an optional 365-day extended reporting period if requested within 60 days of expiration
explanation: MCA 37-51-325 requires policies to include an automatic 60-day extended (tail) reporting period upon termination, plus an option to purchase an additional 365-day extended reporting period if the licensee requests it within 60 days of expiration. The other choices misstate the automatic and optional windows.

question: Under MCA 37-51-325, a Montana licensee who fails to maintain continuous, compliant E&O coverage during licensure is subject to what consequence?
choice_a: Treatment as unprofessional conduct, subjecting the licensee to sanction of the license
choice_b: No consequence unless a client actually files a malpractice claim
choice_c: A civil fine paid directly to the injured party, in lieu of license discipline
choice_d: Automatic conversion of the license to referral-only status
explanation: MCA 37-51-325 makes the failure to maintain continuous, statute-compliant professional liability coverage unprofessional conduct subject to license sanction -- the same enforcement mechanism used elsewhere in the licensing chapter. It does not wait for an actual claim, impose a direct civil fine to the client, or convert the license to a referral-only status.

question: A Montana parcel's legal description reads 'Government Lot 3, Section 14, Township 8 North, Range 5 West, Montana Principal Meridian.' What does the presence of a numbered 'government lot' (rather than a standard quarter-quarter aliquot description) most likely indicate about the parcel?
choice_a: The parcel was created entirely by metes and bounds and has no tie to the rectangular survey
choice_b: The section was irregular -- typically because a river, lake, or other natural feature interrupted the standard quarter-section subdivision -- so the fractional remainder was assigned a lot number instead of an aliquot fraction
choice_c: The parcel is a condominium unit exempt from the Public Land Survey System
choice_d: The description is invalid because government lots were abolished when Montana adopted metric surveying
explanation: Under the Public Land Survey System as applied from the Montana Principal Meridian, a numbered government lot is used where a river, lake shoreline, or other irregularity prevented the section from dividing evenly into standard aliquot quarter-quarters; the fractional piece is described by lot number rather than as (for example) the NE 1/4 of the NW 1/4. It is not evidence of a pure metes-and-bounds description, has nothing to do with condominium status, and government lots remain valid, still-used descriptions in Montana.
source_note: Public Land Survey System as surveyed from the Montana Principal Meridian (established near Three Forks, Gallatin County)

question: All Montana rectangular-survey townships and ranges are measured outward from a single reference point. What is that point called, and generally where is it located?
choice_a: The 6th Principal Meridian, located in Wyoming and shared with Montana by interstate compact
choice_b: The Continental Divide, which serves as both the baseline and meridian for all Montana surveys
choice_c: The Montana Baseline and Montana Principal Meridian, intersecting near the confluence of the Jefferson and Madison rivers southwest of Three Forks
choice_d: Each county seat, which independently anchors its own local township grid
explanation: Montana has its own Principal Meridian and Baseline, with the initial point located near the confluence of the Jefferson and Madison rivers southwest of Three Forks in Gallatin County; all Montana township (north/south of the baseline) and range (east/west of the meridian) designations are measured from that single point. Montana does not use the 6th Principal Meridian, the Continental Divide is not a survey reference line, and there is no county-by-county independent grid.
source_note: Public Land Survey System, Montana Principal Meridian and Baseline

question: A rural Montana parcel with an irregular boundary following an old fence line and a creek, with no clean tie to section lines, is most appropriately described using which method?
choice_a: A government-lot-only description, since irregular boundaries can never use aliquot parts
choice_b: Street address only, since Montana does not require legal descriptions in rural areas
choice_c: A condominium unit description under the Unit Ownership Act
choice_d: Metes and bounds, beginning at a monumented point of beginning and running by courses (bearings) and distances back to that point of beginning
explanation: Metes and bounds -- a point of beginning, sequential courses (bearings) and distances, and closure back to that point -- remains the standard method for describing irregular boundaries that don't align with the rectangular survey grid, and it is used throughout Montana for exactly this kind of parcel. A street address is not a legal description, government lots are a rectangular-survey convention rather than a substitute for metes and bounds, and the Unit Ownership Act applies only to condominiums.
source_note: General land-description convention; contrast with Public Land Survey System descriptions used elsewhere in Montana

question: Under Montana's Unit Ownership Act (MCA Title 70, chapter 23), before a condominium declaration may be recorded in the county where the property is located, what must first occur?
choice_a: The declaration must be approved by the county, which may deny approval only for a noncompliant project name or unpaid taxes/assessments
choice_b: The declaration must be approved by the Montana Board of Realty Regulation
choice_c: A majority of adjoining property owners must consent in writing
choice_d: No approval is required; recording is purely ministerial
explanation: MCA 70-23-304 requires county approval of a condominium declaration before recording, and the county may withhold approval only if the declaration's name doesn't meet MCA 70-23-303's requirements or if taxes/assessments on the property are delinquent. Approval runs through the county, not the real estate board or adjoining owners, and it is not purely automatic.

question: Under Montana's Unit Ownership Act, what governing documents must be created and recorded to establish a condominium, in addition to the declaration itself?
choice_a: Only a plat; bylaws are optional in Montana
choice_b: Bylaws for the association of unit owners, along with floor plans that must be recorded with (and certified as part of) the declaration
choice_c: A partnership agreement filed with the Secretary of State
choice_d: A master deed filed with the IRS in lieu of county recording
explanation: MCA 70-23-306 requires floor plans to be recorded with, and certified as part of, the declaration, and MCA 70-23-307/308 require bylaws for the association of unit owners to be adopted and recorded. Bylaws are not optional, there is no Secretary-of-State partnership filing for condominiums, and there is no IRS master-deed filing requirement.

question: Under the Montana Unit Ownership Act, what restriction applies to the name given to a condominium property in its declaration?
choice_a: There is no restriction on naming
choice_b: The name must include the word 'Condominium' in all capital letters
choice_c: The name may not be so similar to that of another property already on record as to cause confusion or deception
choice_d: The name must match the subdivision plat name exactly, with no variation permitted
explanation: MCA 70-23-303 prohibits a condominium name that is the same as, or so similar to, an existing recorded property name that it tends to confuse or deceive; the county's declaration-approval power under 70-23-304 is tied directly to this naming rule. There is no requirement that 'Condominium' appear in all capitals, and no requirement that the name exactly duplicate the subdivision plat name.

question: Under the Montana Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (MCA 70-24-312), except in an emergency or when impracticable, how much advance notice must a landlord give before entering a tenant's dwelling unit, and under what constraint?
choice_a: 48 hours' notice, and entry is permitted only during business hours Monday through Friday
choice_b: No notice is required as long as the landlord owns the property
choice_c: 72 hours' written notice delivered by certified mail only
choice_d: At least 24 hours' notice, and entry may occur only at reasonable times
explanation: MCA 70-24-312 requires at least 24 hours' notice of intent to enter (waived for emergencies or when impracticable) and limits entry to reasonable times; it does not impose a 48- or 72-hour notice requirement, does not restrict entry to weekday business hours, and does not require certified mail as the sole notice method.

question: Under MCA 70-25-202, after a Montana residential tenancy ends, within how many days must the landlord deliver a written, itemized list of security deposit deductions and return any remaining balance?
choice_a: 30 days
choice_b: 14 days
choice_c: 10 days
choice_d: 60 days
explanation: MCA 70-25-202 gives the landlord 30 days from termination of the tenancy (or the tenant's surrender of the premises, whichever is first) to deliver a written itemized list of deductions and refund the remaining deposit balance. 14, 10, and 60 days are not the statutory figure.

question: Under MCA 70-25-203, what happens if a Montana landlord fails to provide the departing tenant with the written itemized list of deposit deductions required by MCA 70-25-202?
choice_a: The tenant automatically forfeits the entire deposit
choice_b: The landlord forfeits the right to withhold any of the deposit for damages, even if damage actually exists
choice_c: The lease is automatically renewed for another term
choice_d: The landlord may still deduct for damages but must pay a flat $50 penalty
explanation: MCA 70-25-203 provides that a landlord who fails to furnish the itemized list required by 70-25-202 forfeits the right to withhold any portion of the deposit for damages. It does not cause the tenant to forfeit the deposit, does not renew the lease, and Montana law does not substitute a flat $50 penalty for the forfeiture remedy.

question: Under MCA 70-25-201, which of the following is NOT a permitted basis for a Montana landlord to deduct from a residential security deposit?
choice_a: Unpaid rent owed at the end of the tenancy
choice_b: Actual damage to the premises caused by the tenant beyond normal wear and tear
choice_c: Normal cyclical maintenance the landlord would have performed regardless of the tenant's occupancy
choice_d: Cleaning expenses to restore the unit to its condition at the start of the tenancy
explanation: MCA 70-25-201 authorizes deductions for unpaid rent, late charges and lease penalties, tenant-caused damage, and cleaning to restore the unit -- but it specifically bars charging the tenant for normal cyclical maintenance unless the tenant's negligence forced the landlord to perform it out of the ordinary cycle. Choices A-C are all statutorily authorized deductions.

question: A Montana landlord wrongfully withholds a tenant's security deposit in bad faith. Under MCA 70-25-204, what may the tenant recover in a resulting civil action?
choice_a: Only the amount wrongfully withheld, with no additional remedy
choice_b: Automatic punitive damages of three times the monthly rent, regardless of the deposit amount
choice_c: Nothing, because security deposit disputes cannot be litigated in Montana
choice_d: The amount wrongfully withheld plus court costs and reasonable attorney's fees
explanation: MCA 70-25-204 allows a tenant to recover the wrongfully withheld amount plus court costs and reasonable attorney's fees. It is not limited to bare repayment of the withheld sum, does not impose an automatic treble-rent penalty, and deposit disputes are of course litigable.

question: A Montana lender forecloses a mortgage on a 60-acre ranch parcel by judicial foreclosure and execution sale under Title 25. Under MCA 71-1-228 and MCA 25-13-802, what redemption right does the borrower (judgment debtor) have after the sale?
choice_a: The right to redeem the property from the purchaser within 1 year after the sale, by paying the purchase price plus interest and specified costs
choice_b: No post-sale redemption right; the sale is final immediately
choice_c: The right to redeem within 90 days only, with no ability to recover taxes paid by the purchaser
choice_d: A perpetual redemption right with no time limit
explanation: MCA 71-1-228 extends the redemption rights applicable to execution sales to mortgage and deed-of-trust power-of-sale foreclosures (other than Small Tract Financing Act trust indenture sales), and MCA 25-13-802 sets that redemption window at 1 year after the sale, requiring reimbursement of the purchase price plus interest, taxes paid, and other specified costs. There is no immediate finality, no 90-day-only window, and no perpetual right.

question: A Montana borrower secures a home loan on a 5-acre lot with a deed of trust (trust indenture) under the Small Tract Financing Act. If the trustee forecloses nonjudicially and sells the property, what happens to the borrower's post-sale redemption rights, and what acreage limit makes the Act available in the first place?
choice_a: The borrower keeps the standard 1-year post-sale redemption right; the Act applies to any acreage
choice_b: The Act is available only for parcels of 40 acres or less, and MCA 71-1-228 specifically excludes trust indenture sales under the Act from the post-sale redemption rights that apply to other mortgage and execution sales
choice_c: The Act applies only to parcels over 40 acres, and the borrower gets a 2-year redemption period
choice_d: The Act has no acreage limit, but redemption is extended to 3 years for trust indenture sales
explanation: MCA 71-1-304 limits trust indentures under the Small Tract Financing Act to real property not exceeding 40 acres, and MCA 71-1-228 expressly carves out power-of-sale trust indenture sales under that Act from the post-sale redemption rights otherwise available on mortgage and execution sales -- meaning there is no post-sale redemption once a nonjudicial trustee's sale under the Act is completed. The other choices invert the acreage limit or invent redemption periods that don't exist for these sales.

question: A Montana borrower in default under a Small Tract Financing Act trust indenture wants to stop a scheduled nonjudicial trustee's sale. Under MCA 71-1-312, what may the borrower do before the sale occurs?
choice_a: Nothing; once notice of sale is recorded, the sale cannot be stopped
choice_b: Pay the entire remaining loan balance in full, which is the only way to halt the sale
choice_c: Pay the amount actually in default (reinstating the loan), which discontinues the foreclosure proceeding
choice_d: Redeem the property only after the sale is completed, within 1 year
explanation: MCA 71-1-312 allows a defaulting grantor to cure by paying the amount actually in default before the trustee's sale, which discontinues the foreclosure proceeding (a right to reinstate rather than pay off the entire loan). This pre-sale cure is available -- it isn't true that nothing can stop the sale, full payoff of the whole loan isn't required, and (as reflected in MCA 71-1-228) there is no post-sale redemption period for trust indenture sales under this Act.

question: Under Montana's statute of frauds for real property (MCA 70-20-101), what does a transfer of an interest in real property generally require to be valid, and what is the narrow exception?
choice_a: A notarized deed only; a signed private writing without notarization is void
choice_b: Oral agreement is always sufficient if two witnesses are present
choice_c: Recording with the county clerk is the only requirement; a signature is not necessary
choice_d: An instrument in writing signed by the party creating or transferring the interest (or that party's agent, authorized in writing), except for an estate at will or a term not exceeding 1 year
explanation: MCA 70-20-101 requires a conveyance or other instrument in writing, subscribed by the transferring party or the party's lawful agent authorized in writing, with a specific exception for an estate at will or a term not exceeding 1 year. Notarization is not what makes an instrument valid under this statute, oral agreements with witnesses do not substitute for the writing, and recording is a separate act from the writing/signature requirement.

question: Under MCA 70-20-102, Montana's statute of frauds for real property does NOT prevent which of the following, even absent a signed writing?
choice_a: A court compelling specific performance of an agreement where there has been partial performance, or a trust arising or being extinguished by operation of law
choice_b: Enforcement of an unsigned commercial lease exceeding 1 year
choice_c: A licensee collecting commission on an oral listing agreement
choice_d: A buyer forcing a seller to convey based solely on a verbal promise with no partial performance
explanation: MCA 70-20-102 carves out testamentary dispositions, trusts arising or extinguished by implication or operation of law, and a court's power to compel specific performance where there has been partial performance of an agreement -- these survive despite the writing requirement. It does not validate an unsigned long-term commercial lease, does not create a commission right on a purely oral listing, and does not allow enforcement of a bare verbal promise with no partial performance.

question: A Montana landlord and tenant orally agree to a 9-month residential lease with no written document. Under the statute of frauds framework applied to real property (MCA 70-20-101), is this lease enforceable without a writing?
choice_a: No -- any lease of any length must be in writing in Montana
choice_b: Yes -- MCA 70-20-101 exempts an estate at will or for a term not exceeding 1 year from the writing requirement, so a 9-month oral lease falls within that exception
choice_c: No -- only leases of exactly 6 months or less are exempt
choice_d: Yes, but only if the rent is paid entirely in advance
explanation: MCA 70-20-101 exempts an estate at will or a term not exceeding 1 year from the general writing requirement for real property interests, so a 9-month oral residential lease falls within that statutory exception and can be enforceable without a writing. It is not true that all leases must be written, the exception is not capped at 6 months, and advance payment of rent is not what makes the oral term valid.
